analysis.one_liner: Raises tax penalties on corporations using tax havens and gives federal contracts to companies that don't offshore jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to publish a list of countries it considers corporate tax havens, then sharply increased the tax penalties corporations face for hiding money or committing fraud involving those countries — for example, raising the penalty for understating tax tied to an undisclosed foreign asset from 20% to 60%. It also would have let federal agencies favor contractors that have not laid off a U.S. worker and moved that same job to a foreign country, with fines and a two-year ban on federal contracting for lying about it. Money raised would have been set aside to reduce the federal debt.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. workers whose jobs are at risk of being offshored gain, because federal agencies could preferentially hire contractors that keep those jobs here. Honest taxpayers gain from tougher penalties on corporations that shift profits or hide assets in tax havens. The Treasury gains revenue that would be dedicated to reducing the federal debt.

how_it_helps.text: It directs Treasury to publish and periodically update a list of corporate tax haven countries, using criteria like low tax rates, weak information-sharing, and low financial transparency [S2][S3].

It raises penalties for corporations that understate tax, commit fraud, or make false statements involving tax haven countries — for example, from 20% to 60% for underpayments tied to an undisclosed foreign asset in a haven, from 75% to 100% for fraud, and doubling several criminal fine maximums [S2][S3].

It lets federal departments and agencies give preference in contract awards to companies that did not engage in outsourcing the prior year, and requires them to ask every bidder whether they offshored jobs; lying about it can bring a penalty up to the contract's value and a two-year debarment from federal contracting [S2][S3].
Revenue raised under the bill must be set aside to reduce the public debt [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that use tax haven countries to shelter profits or hide assets would face much larger penalties, and compliance costs would rise as companies must disclose whether they have offshored jobs when bidding for federal contracts. Federal contractors that have offshored jobs could lose bid preferences.

drawbacks.text: The outsourcing preference applies only to federal contracts and the definition is narrow — it covers only laying off a U.S. worker and moving that exact job abroad [S2][S3] — so it would do little for the many other ways jobs and work move offshore, and honest supporters would concede it is a modest tool against a large phenomenon.

The bill leaves the tax haven list to the Treasury Secretary's discretion using broad criteria [S3], so companies would face sharply higher penalties on transactions involving countries the Secretary designates — a compliance burden and litigation risk that a fair-minded skeptic would flag as a cost, even for firms trying to comply.
Contractors would bear new disclosure obligations in every federal bidding process, and a false statement could cost up to the contract's value plus a two-year debarment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary taxpayers and workers, the benefits are real but targeted: tougher penalties on haven-based evasion and a modest hiring preference for companies that keep jobs onshore. The main costs fall on multinational corporations and federal contractors in the form of higher penalties and compliance burdens, which is where the bill intends them to fall. The bill would not stop offshoring broadly — it works only at the margins of federal contracting and haven-country tax enforcement — so it is a worthwhile but limited measure, not a comprehensive answer to either problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Oversight committees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever acted on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on July 13, 2017 and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so any bill not enacted by then dies and must be reintroduced from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations that shift profits or assets to tax haven countries are better off, since the higher penalties never took effect, and federal contractors that have offshored jobs keep equal footing in bidding. Taxpayers whose taxes subsidize the enforcement gap are worse off.

for.name: Rep. Jerry McNerney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary referral; chaired by Rep. Kevin Brady (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never took it up — no hearing, markup, or vote during the 115th Congress

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never considered the bill

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so it never developed enough support for a party split to show; the outcome was decided by committee inaction rather than any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill directly targets corporations that move profits, assets, or transactions into tax haven countries, tripling some underpayment penalties and doubling criminal fine exposure for haven-linked offenses. Its defeat leaves the existing 20% penalty structure in place.

Contractors that keep jobs onshore would gain a bidding preference; contractors that lay off a U.S. worker and move that job abroad would lose the preference and face new disclosure rules. Either way, all bidders would carry new compliance costs.

industries.industry: Offshore financial services and tax haven jurisdictions
industries.note: Countries designated as corporate tax havens would become markers for sharply higher penalties on transactions routed through them, reducing their appeal as destinations for corporate money.
